zh.independent_solution: A passive lossy circuit cannot sustain oscillations from a finite initial energy supply. Periodic external emf supplies the drive. In a steady periodic state the stored electrical/magnetic energy is the same at the beginning and end of each cycle, so integrating the energy balance gives external net work per cycle equal to resistive heat loss. A one-time charge gives a decaying transient; constant DC gives a nonoscillatory steady response. The complete required-condition set is A,D.

option_checks.evidence: Continuing periodically varying external emf provides the forcing; its repeated drive remains after any free transient decays.

With no source after the initial charge, every cycle dissipates energy in R. An initial capacitor charge therefore cannot maintain the specified steady oscillation; this is free decay, not sustained forcing.
The applied emf has no periodic variation. For a passive stable lossy linear circuit its startup transient decays and a DC steady state does not provide continuing alternating oscillations.
Periodicity gives Delta E_stored=0 over a cycle. Energy conservation then requires W_external=integral R i(t)^2 dt, replacing that cycle's resistive loss rather than allowing amplitude decay.

zh.independent_solution: For constant R>0, u(t)=R i(t). Setting i(t)=I_m sin(omega t+phi) gives u(t)=R I_m sin(omega t+phi), with identical phase and simultaneous zeros/extrema. No quarter-period shift or minus sign can represent this fixed pure resistor. Only C is true.

option_checks.evidence: Although u=Ri is right, a quarter-cycle voltage lead would put a voltage extremum at a current zero, contradicting instantaneous u=Ri.
A quarter-cycle current lead likewise separates zeros and extrema. Multiplication by a positive constant R cannot shift the sinusoid's phase.
Positive proportionality u=Ri gives both the correct instantaneous Ohm law and the same phase for voltage and current.
At i=I_m>0 a passive resistor has u=R I_m>0, not -R I_m. The minus sign and half-cycle difference both describe the wrong relation.

zh.independent_solution: Over the stated period T, I=sqrt((1/T) integral i(t)^2 dt) and U=sqrt((1/T) integral u(t)^2 dt), with nonnegative roots. Squaring precedes the time average. For i=sin(omega t) the signed mean is zero while RMS is 1/sqrt(2); for u=sin(omega t) the largest absolute voltage is 1 while RMS is 1/sqrt(2). Hence the complete true definition set is A,C, regardless of accidental equality for special waveforms.

option_checks.evidence: The formula averages i^2, not i, over the defined period and takes the nonnegative square root, giving current units back after averaging squared current.
For any nonzero symmetric sinusoidal current, overline(i)=0 but sqrt(overline(i^2))=I_m/sqrt(2)>0. Signed mean is therefore not a general RMS definition.
The same operation order applied to u puts u^2 inside the time average and the nonnegative square root outside; this is voltage RMS.
A sinusoidal voltage with peak U_m>0 has max|u|=U_m and RMS=U_m/sqrt(2). A peak can equal RMS for special constant-magnitude waveforms, but cannot define RMS for periodic voltages generally.

en.independent_solution: Under the English stem's passive, resistively lossy, steady-periodic assumptions, continued oscillation needs external periodic forcing. At the cycle endpoints the circuit has identical stored energy. The integrated work-energy relation is zero stored-energy change equals source work minus resistive heat, so the source's net work must replace the heat each cycle. Initial capacitor charge is exhausted by loss, and constant DC has no continuing periodic drive. All and only A,D satisfy the requested conditions.

option_checks.evidence: The continually applied periodically varying emf is precisely an external drive producing forced rather than isolated free oscillations.
After the one-time charge there is no external work input. Positive resistive heating reduces the available stored energy; oscillations decay instead of reaching a sustained periodic amplitude.
Constant magnitude and direction describe DC, not an oscillatory drive. Any switch-on oscillation is a transient, not the assumed continuing forced periodic response.

The net energy supplied per cycle equals that cycle's resistive heat because the steady-periodic stored energy returns to its initial value. This is necessary maintenance, not equality of instantaneous powers.

No sinusoidal-only peak rule is being treated as a definition for arbitrary waveforms.
